name: Howlite
physical: Kept nearby for comfort during stressful times
Crystal healers link it to relaxation of muscle tension
summary: Howlite is a chalky white borate with grey veining, often dyed blue as turquoise, used in crystal tradition for calm, patience and a quiet mind.
intro: Howlite is a soft, chalky white stone threaded with fine grey or black veins that look like spider webs. In its natural form it forms nodules that resemble cauliflower heads, and polished beads can resemble marble. The same porous surface takes dye very easily, which is why bright turquoise howlite is so common in beads and cabochons. At just 3.5 on the Mohs scale, it is easy to carve into animals, boxes and beads. Beyond looks, it is cherished by crystal lovers as a calming stone for hectic times.
history: Howlite was first discovered in 1868 by Canadian geologist Henry How in Nova Scotia, who found the nodules inside gypsum beds, and it was named in his honor. Later, large deposits in California's Tick Canyon became a major source. Its tendency to be dyed to resemble turquoise earned the nickname white turquoise. Carving workshops in Europe and Asia use it as an affordable ornamental stone. As with many borates, there is no old folklore tied to howlite, and its metaphysical meaning is modern.
meaning: Crystal healers consider howlite a stone of patience and calm. Its soft white tones are linked to the crown and third eye, and people use it to cool anger, interrupt anxious loops and settle into meditation. It is associated with restful sleep, and a piece on the nightstand is said to help the mind wind down. Practitioners also describe it as a study aid, helping you stay patient with difficult material. Emotionally it is tied to awareness of habits, such as snapping or rushing, so you can respond instead of react. Traditionally it is linked to relaxed muscles and a quiet body. Dyed blue howlite is often used as a budget stand-in for turquoise.
howToUse: Place a howlite stone on the nightstand or under the pillow for a calm bedtime routine. Hold a tumbled piece in your palm when you feel your temper rise, and breathe slowly until the stone warms. Use it during study sessions to keep a patient frame of mind. In meditation, rest it on the brow. If you wear howlite beads, remove them before bathing and swimming. A bowl of white howlite on the desk makes a gentle reminder to pause.
care: Howlite is soft and porous, so water can dull its surface and wash out dye. Avoid soaking and wipe with a soft dry cloth. Cleanse with sound, breath, smoke or moonlight. Strong sun is usually fine for natural white pieces, but keep dyed blue ones in shade to protect the color. Store separately to prevent scratches. Avoid ultrasonic cleaners, chemicals and perfumes.
identify: Natural howlite is white with grey to black veining, chalky and lightweight, and scratches with a knife. It is commonly dyed blue to imitate turquoise, and dye often collects in cracks or rubs off with acetone. Real turquoise is harder, has a more waxy luster and veins that are brown or matrix, not black spider webs. Howlite is also dyed pink, green and purple. Magnesite looks similar, but is harder.

faq.a: Howlite is naturally white, but it is porous and takes dye easily, so it is frequently dyed blue to imitate turquoise. Look for dye in cracks or on the surface and ask sellers whether the stone is natural.
In crystal tradition howlite is used for calm, patience and restful sleep. People keep it on the nightstand, hold it when angry or anxious, and place it on desks to support patient study.
Avoid it. Howlite is soft and porous, and water can dull the surface and wash out dye. Wipe it dry and cleanse with moonlight, sound or breath instead.
